A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CityNav. Their main text, tables, figures, equations, and appendices are readable and support matching retained content across the substantial revision.

before.justification: v2 reports original navigation benchmarks, human performance, ablations, training-size experiments, and disaster/GNSS robustness results in Sections 4 and Appendix D.

after.justification: v3 reports original navigation experiments, map-component ablations, robustness evaluations, and analyses of trajectories, descriptions, landmarks, and object categories.

M1.justification: v2 centers on MGP, which predicts goal coordinates and progress, executes movements toward predicted goals, and optionally refines destinations using LLaVA/Set-of-Mark prompting. v3 instead supplies GSM features to recurrent action-prediction policies, including CMA+GSM and AerialVLN+GSM (Section 4; Appendix C). The five map categories and earlier MapSeq2Seq approach are retained within this substantial architectural and procedural revision.

E1.justification: The CityNav corpus and urban navigation task remain, as do flooding and unreliable-GNSS evaluations. Earthquake-induced ground-fissure testing, present in v2 Tables 6 and 12, is absent from v3, which leaves other disaster types for future work.

E2.justification: v3 separately evaluates AerialVLN and adds CMA+GSM and AerialVLN+GSM, while Random and MGP disappear from the comparison set. Seq2Seq+GSM corresponds to v2's MapSeq2Seq. The flood comparison also changes from MGP trained with shortest paths or demonstrations to six models with and without GSM (v3 Table 7).

E3.justification: v3 specifies uniform five-epoch Adam training at 1.5e-3 with batch size 12, replacing the separately budgeted MGP experiments using ten-epoch AdamW training at 1e-3 with batch size 8. Training-size and ablation studies change models and move from validation-unseen to test-unseen. OSR changes from a planar distance criterion to spherical success, and data filtering is redescribed using success criteria instead of v2's 30-meter cutoff. These are reported protocol revisions; reruns or recollection are not established.

E4.justification: v3 adds trajectory-landmark proximity analysis, description-length and landmark-count stratifications, and category-level performance analysis (Figure 7, Figures 9–10, Appendices B and D). It removes v2's distance-difficulty analyses in Tables 3, 9, and 10. Map ablations change from combined target/surroundings and view/explored-channel removals to separate potential-goal and surrounding-object removals, alongside revised robustness experiments.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and descriptive distributions without stated experimental run or seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bars. The added analyses do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Substantial result sets are added or replaced for the revised models and analyses; v3 Table 2 reports test-unseen SR of 6.72% for AerialVLN+GSM. The matched MapSeq2Seq/Seq2Seq+GSM test-unseen SR changes from 4.59% in v2 Table 11 to 3.81% in v3 Table 2, while its validation rows remain identical. The main HD-trained Seq2Seq, CMA, and Human rows are also retained. Method and protocol revisions prevent interpreting the revision as a same-setting performance improvement.

T1.justification: The geometric definition of oracle success changes: v2 Section 4.1 uses proximity within 20 meters on the xy-plane, whereas v3 Section 3.2 uses the 20-meter spherical success region. This revises the mathematical acceptance criterion. Neither version contains a theorem or proof development.

C1.justification: The CityNav dataset contribution remains, but the central methodological contribution is redefined. v2 emphasizes a proposed goal-prediction model outperforming existing agents; v3 claims a reusable GSM representation that improves three existing navigation architectures. This substantially broadens the methodological claim beyond the specialized MGP baseline.

C2.justification: v2 interprets target/surroundings maps as minimally useful because of detector viewpoint mismatch; v3 interprets its revised model's ablations as showing benefits from every tested component. New description and landmark analyses support additional mechanism explanations. Limitations shift from physical interactions, dynamic objects, and privacy concerns to limited city coverage and scanning costs, with new multi-agent and cross-domain research directions.

D1.justification: v3 adds exact GSM convolutional-layer specifications, map resolution, loss descriptions, and look-ahead step size 10. v2's detection thresholds, cached-map construction recipe, and several embedding details are omitted. Hardware changes from H100 for Seq2Seq/CMA to RTX 4090 for all models. v3 also introduces conflicting learning-rate disclosures: 1.5e-3 in Section 5.1 versus 5 in Appendix C.3. The project URL remains unchanged.

R1.justification: The literature coverage is substantially refreshed with works such as EmbodiedCity, OpenFly, recent realistic UAV navigation, NavGPT, and NavID, while much of v2's conventional UAV control, rescue, and GNSS discussion is removed. v3 also distinguishes CMA from AerialVLN's look-ahead extension, revising their relationship in the paper's positioning.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose is rewritten, with dedicated Task Definition and Models sections and substantial reorganization of experiments and appendices. The title changes, the simulator is named CityFlight, and the narrative is rebuilt around reusable GSM inputs and comparisons across architectures.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, redesigns the dataset-comparison table, reorganizes statistics plots, and replaces MGP diagrams with GSM and recurrent-policy illustrations. New analysis charts and category tables are added. The six qualitative examples in v2 Appendix Figure 12 are retained and relocated to v3 Figure 11.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens the evidence through systematic comparisons with and without GSM, new contextual analyses, and clearer organization. However, it removes difficulty and earthquake analyses and introduces unresolved reporting problems. Section 5.1 and Appendix C.3 disagree on the learning rate, while Appendix D claims all models worsen under flooding despite AerialVLN+GSM showing better values on all four metrics in Table 7 than in Table 2. The broader evidence is valuable, but these reproducibility and interpretation problems prevent a confident net quality judgment.
